clinicalPearls: A recognisable pattern of agitated delirium, dilated pupils, dry flushed skin, urinary retention, reduced bowel sounds and fever
The classic teaching mnemonic describes the patient as hot, dry, flushed, blind, mad and full (of urine)
Common causes include antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, antipsychotics, antimuscarinic agents and certain plants
The dry skin and absent bowel sounds help distinguish it from the sympathomimetic toxidrome, in which the patient sweats
Management is largely supportive with sedation for agitation, and physostigmine may be used in selected cases
Hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis from agitation are important complications to prevent and treat
reference.pathophysiology: The anticholinergic toxidrome results from blockade of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, both centrally and peripherally. Central blockade produces agitation, delirium and hallucinations, while peripheral blockade causes mydriasis, tachycardia, reduced sweating with dry flushed skin, urinary retention and decreased gut motility. Impaired sweating undermines heat loss and predisposes to dangerous hyperthermia, and the constellation reflects loss of normal parasympathetic muscarinic tone.
additionalDifferentials: Sepsis or CNS infection causing delirium
additionalInvestigations: Clinical recognition of the toxidrome and a careful medication and exposure history
Electrocardiogram, particularly to detect tricyclic-related conduction changes
Temperature monitoring and creatine kinase for hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis
Exclusion of infective and other metabolic causes of delirium
redFlags: Wide QRS or arrhythmia suggesting tricyclic toxicity
Severe agitation risking injury or rhabdomyolysis
reference.prognosis: With supportive care and control of agitation and temperature most patients recover fully; outcome worsens with severe hyperthermia, arrhythmia or complications of the underlying overdose.
pitfalls: Confusing it with the sympathomimetic toxidrome (dry versus sweaty skin)
Missing urinary retention as a cause of ongoing agitation
Using physostigmine inappropriately, especially with tricyclic overdose
management: Give supportive care as the mainstay: secure the airway, provide intravenous fluids and institute continuous cardiac monitoring
Control agitation and limit hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis risk with benzodiazepine sedation rather than physical restraint alone
Consider physostigmine as a specific antimuscarinic antidote for pure central anticholinergic delirium, avoiding it where tricyclic co-ingestion or cardiac conduction delay is suspected
Treat hyperthermia promptly with active external cooling alongside aggressive fluid resuscitation
Relieve urinary retention by bladder catheterisation and support impaired bowel motility
Where tricyclic ingestion produces QRS prolongation or arrhythmia, treat with intravenous sodium bicarbonate
Consider activated charcoal for a recent significant ingestion, and monitor creatine kinase to detect and fluid-treat rhabdomyolysis
Liaise with clinical toxicology or the poisons service and observe until the toxidrome resolves
